payload.description: Hermes WebUI: The best way to use Hermes Agent from the web or from your phone!

payload.text:
# Hermes Web UI [Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) is a sophisticated autonomous agent that lives on your server, accessed via a terminal or messaging apps, that remembers what it learns and gets more capable the longer it runs. Hermes WebUI is a lightweight, dark-themed web app interface in your browser for [Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/). Full parity with the CLI experience - everything you can do from a terminal, you can do from this UI. No build step, no framework, no bundler. Just Python and vanilla JS. Layout: three-panel. Left sidebar for sessions and navigation, center for chat, right for workspace file browsing. Model, profile, and workspace controls live in the **composer footer** — always visible while composing. A circular context ring shows token usage at a glance. All settings and session tools are in the **Hermes Control Center** (launcher at the sidebar bottom).

Light mode with full profile support
Customize your settings, configure a password

Workspace file browser with inline preview
Session projects, tags, and tool call cards
This gives you nearly **1:1 parity with Hermes CLI from a convenient web UI** which you can access securely through an SSH tunnel from your Hermes setup. Single command to start this up, and a single command to SSH tunnel for access on your computer. Every single part of the web UI uses your existing Hermes agent and existing models, without requiring any additional setup. --- ## Why Hermes Most AI tools reset every session. They don't know who you are, what you worked on, or what conventions your project follows. You re-explain yourself every time. Hermes retains context across sessions, runs scheduled jobs while you're offline, and gets smarter about your environment the longer it runs. It uses your existing Hermes agent setup, your existing models, and requires no additional configuration to start. What makes it different from other agentic tools: - **Persistent memory** — user profile, agent notes, and a skills system that saves reusable procedures; Hermes learns your environment and does not have to relearn it - **Self-hosted scheduling** — cron jobs that fire while you're offline and deliver results to Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, email, and more - **10+ messaging platforms** — the same agent available in the terminal is reachable from your phone - **Self-improving skills** — Hermes writes and saves its own skills automatically from experience; no marketplace to browse, no plugins to install - **Provider-agnostic** — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, and more - **Orchestrates other agents** — can spawn Claude Code or Codex for heavy coding tasks and bring the results back into its own memory - **Self-hosted** — your conversations, your memory, your hardware **vs. the field** *(landscape is actively shifting — see [docs/why-hermes.md](docs/why-hermes.md) for the full breakdown)*: | | OpenClaw | Claude Code | Codex CLI | OpenCode | Hermes | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Persistent memory (auto) | Yes | Partial† | Partial | Partial | Yes | | Scheduled jobs (self-hosted) | Yes | No‡ | No | No | Yes | | Messaging app access | Yes (15+ platforms) | Partial (Telegram/Discord preview) | No | No | Yes (10+) | | Web UI (self-hosted) | Dashboard only | No | No | Yes | Yes | | Self-improving skills | Partial | No | No | No | Yes | | Python / ML ecosystem | No (Node.js) | No | No | No | Yes | | Provider-agnostic | Yes | No (Claude only) | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Open source | Yes (MIT) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | † Claude Code has CLAUDE.md / MEMORY.md project context and rolling auto-memory, but not full automatic cross-session recall ‡ Claude Code has cloud-managed scheduling (Anthropic infrastructure) and session-scoped `/loop`; no self-hosted cron **The closest competitor is OpenClaw** — both are always-on, self-hosted, open-source agents with memory, cron, and messaging. The key differences: Hermes writes and saves its own skills automatically as a core behavior (OpenClaw's skill system centers on a community marketplace); Hermes is more stable across updates (OpenClaw has documented release regressions and ClawHub has had security incidents involving malicious skills); and Hermes runs natively in the Python ecosystem. See [docs/why-hermes.md](docs/why-hermes.md) for the full side-by-side. --- ## Quick start Run the repo bootstrap: ```bash git clone https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui.git hermes-webui cd hermes-webui python3 bootstrap.py ``` Or keep using the shell launcher: ```bash ./start.sh ``` For self-hosted VM or homelab installs, `ctl.sh` wraps the common daemon lifecycle commands without requiring `fuser` or `pkill`: ```bash ./ctl.sh start # background daemon, PID at ~/.hermes/webui.pid ./ctl.sh status # PID, uptime, bound host/port, log path, /health ./ctl.sh logs --lines 100 # tail ~/.hermes/webui.log ./ctl.sh restart ./ctl.sh stop ``` `ctl.sh start` runs the bootstrap in foreground/no-browser mode behind the daemon wrapper, writes logs to `~/.hermes/webui.log`, and respects `.env` plus inline overrides such as `HERMES_WEBUI_HOST=0.0.0.0 ./ctl.sh start`. ### Optional session recall prefill WebUI can attach ephemeral prefill messages to new browser-originated agent turns. This is useful when a deployment already has a local recall or router script for Joplin, Obsidian, Notion, llm-wiki, or another third-party notes source and wants browser chat to know where durable context lives. Prefer a compact router-style prefill (for example, "Joplin has the durable project context; use the available notes/search tools before answering detail-dependent questions") instead of dumping the full note corpus into every new browser session. The prefill should point the agent toward retrieval; the notes/search tools should provide the specific facts on demand. Static JSON remains supported through `prefill_messages_file` or `HERMES_PREFILL_MESSAGES_FILE`. For dynamic recall, opt in explicitly with a WebUI-specific script hook: ```yaml webui_prefill_messages_script: - python3 - /path/to/notes_recall.py webui_prefill_messages_script_timeout: 5 ``` or: ```bash HERMES_WEBUI_PREFILL_MESSAGES_SCRIPT="python3 /path/to/notes_recall.py" \ HERMES_WEBUI_PREFILL_MESSAGES_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT=5 \ ./ctl.sh restart ``` The script may print either an OpenAI-style JSON message list, a JSON object with a `messages` list, or plain text; plain text is wrapped as one `user` prefill message so dynamic recall text becomes ordinary context instead of an extra system instruction. If the hook must provide system-level guidance, emit JSON messages with an explicit `role: "system"` entry instead. Script output is capped at 256 KiB before parsing. Parsed prefill context is then bounded by `webui_prefill_context_max_chars` or `HERMES_WEBUI_PREFILL_CONTEXT_MAX_CHARS` (default: 12,000 characters; set to `0` to disable). When a dynamic script exceeds the budget and a compact static prefill file is configured, WebUI falls back to that file. If no compact fallback is available, WebUI injects a short retrieval instruction instead of sending the oversized note/body payload with every new browser turn. The browser only receives a compact status event (`source`, `label`, message count, compaction metadata, and redacted errors), never the prefill message bodies. ### Optional Gateway-backed browser chat By default, browser chat runs through WebUI's in-process legacy runtime. Advanced self-hosted deployments can opt into routing new browser turns through a running Hermes Gateway API server while preserving the existing WebUI `/api/chat/start` and `/api/chat/stream` browser contract: ```bash HERMES_WEBUI_CHAT_BACKEND=gateway \ HERMES_WEBUI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8642 \ HERMES_WEBUI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=... \ ./ctl.sh restart ``` `HERMES_WEBUI_CHAT_BACKEND` is intentionally strict: only `gateway`, `api_server`, or `api-server` enable the bridge. Generic truthy values such as `1` or `true` are ignored so existing deployments do not change execution ownership accidentally. If `HERMES_WEBUI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` is omitted, WebUI falls back to `API_SERVER_KEY` when present. When Gateway returns HTTP 401, WebUI reports a `gateway_auth_error` that points at this WebUI↔Gateway key mismatch rather than showing the Gateway's generic provider-style "Invalid API key" body. `/api/health/agent` also includes a redacted `gateway_chat` block so operators can see whether gateway mode, base URL, and API-key presence are configured without exposing the key value. That `gateway_chat` field is an operator diagnostic payload only; it is not currently rendered as a user-facing health banner in the browser UI. The bridge is best used by operators who already run Hermes Gateway/API Server locally and want browser-originated chat to use the same runtime/tool path as messaging surfaces. Attachments, cancellation, approvals, and clarify prompts still follow WebUI's current compatibility path and may not match every messaging surface until the runtime-adapter migration is complete. The bootstrap will: 1. Detect Hermes Agent and, if missing, attempt the official installer (`curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash`). 2. Find or create a Python environment with the WebUI dependencies. 3. Start the web server and wait for `/health`. 4. Open the browser unless you pass `--no-browser`. 5. Drop you into a first-run onboarding wizard inside the WebUI. > Native Windows is not supported for this bootstrap yet. Use Linux, macOS, or WSL2. > For Windows / WSL auto-start at login, see [`docs/wsl-autostart.md`](docs/wsl-autostart.md). A community-maintained native Windows setup is documented at [@markwang2658/hermes-windows-native-guide](https://github.com/markwang2658/hermes-windows-native-guide) (companion setup repo: [@markwang2658/hermes-windows-native](https://github.com/markwang2658/hermes-windows-native)). Notes from the community report in [#1952](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/issues/1952): - **Memory:** community-measured ~330 MB native vs ~1080 MB with WSL2+Docker (varies by configuration). - **What works:** chat, workspace browser, session management, all themes. - **Known limitations:** some POSIX-style file paths surface in the workspace browser; bash-assuming agent tools may not work natively. - **Native Windows setup:** install Python 3.11+, then from the hermes-agent root in PowerShell: `python -m venv venv` → `pip install -r requirements.txt` → `pwsh .\start.ps1` (it auto-discovers `venv\Scripts\python.exe`). - **WSL2 relationship:** not a prerequisite — a WSL2-built venv (`venv/bin/python`, ELF) isn't invokable by native Windows Python, so use the native setup above. WSL2 stays useful as a parallel install if you want the full `bootstrap.py` + Linux runtime. If provider setup is still incomplete af

# Contributing to Hermes WebUI

Thanks for contributing.

Hermes WebUI is intentionally simple to work on: Python on the server, vanilla JS in the browser, no build step, no bundler, no frontend framework. The best pull requests preserve that simplicity while solving a real problem cleanly.

## Before You Start

- Read [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) if an AI assistant is doing or helping with the
  change.
- Read [`docs/CONTRACTS.md`](docs/CONTRACTS.md) and any linked contract/RFC for
  the subsystem you will touch.
- For UI or UX work, read [`docs/UIUX-GUIDE.md`](docs/UIUX-GUIDE.md)
  and [`DESIGN.md`](DESIGN.md).
- For runtime, streaming, recovery, replay, compression, context reconstruction,
  or session metadata work, start with [`docs/rfcs/README.md`](docs/rfcs/README.md)
  and the relevant RFC listed there.

Use those documents as review guardrails: keep the change scoped, preserve the
no-build-step architecture, update docs/changelog when behavior changes, include
UI evidence for UI changes, and add tests for behavior changes where practical.

### Contract-affecting PRs

A contract-affecting PR is any change that updates a public contract document,
an RFC, a contributor guide, a product-semantics test, or behavior that those
documents already describe. These PRs need an explicit `Contract Routing` section
in the PR body that names the touched contract family and the evidence used.
See [`docs/CONTRACTS.md#contract-routing`](docs/CONTRACTS.md#contract-routing)
for the short routing shape and [`docs/CONTRACTS.md#contract-changes`](docs/CONTRACTS.md#contract-changes)
for intentional contract changes.

If the PR intentionally changes an existing contract, add a `Contract Change`
section that states the old rule, the new rule, and why the change is justified.
Do not silently redefine product behavior by changing tests alone; update the
corresponding docs in the same PR.

A release batch should call out included contract-affecting PRs separately
from ordinary fixes, even when the code diff is small and CI is green.

## Two Paths to a Strong Pull Request

### Path 1: Small, Focused Changes

This is the fastest path to review and merge.

- Fix one clear bug or add one tightly scoped improvement
- Touch the fewest files you can
- Avoid drive-by refactors mixed into functional changes
- Run the relevant tests locally before opening the PR
- Keep the PR description concise and specific

These are the changes that are easiest to review and safest to merge quickly.

### Path 2: Bigger Changes

If you want to change architecture, reshape a workflow, add a substantial UI feature, or alter core behavior, align on direction first.

- Open an issue, start a discussion, or open a draft PR early
- Explain the problem you are solving, not just the implementation you want
- Call out tradeoffs, migration risk, and any alternatives you considered
- Keep the final PR easy to review by separating unrelated work

Large changes are welcome, but surprise rewrites are hard to review well.

## What We Expect in Every PR

### 1. One Logical Change Per PR

Keep each PR focused. A small related group of fixes is fine. A bug fix plus a CSS cleanup plus a refactor plus a docs rewrite is not.

### 2. Local Verification

Run the test suite locally:

```bash
pytest tests/ -v --timeout=60
```

CI also runs this suite on Python `3.11`, `3.12`, and `3.13`.

If your change affects browser behavior, also run the relevant manual checks from [TESTING.md](TESTING.md).

### 3. Clear PR Description

There is currently no PR template in this repo, so include the important sections yourself:

- Thinking Path
- What Changed
- Why It Matters
- Verification
- Risks / Follow-ups
- Model Used

If the change is user-visible, include screenshots or a short video.

For UI or UX changes, before/after images are required. PRs that change the interface or interaction flow without before/after images may not receive meaningful review until that evidence is added.

### 4. AI Usage Disclosure

If AI helped produce the change, say so in the PR description.

Include:

- Provider
- Exact model name or ID
- Any notable mode or tool use that mattered

If no AI was used, write: `None — human-authored`.

### 5. Keep the Docs Honest

If your change alters behavior, architecture, testing, setup, or user-facing workflows, update the relevant docs in the same PR.

Common files:

- [README.md](README.md) for setup, usage, and contributor-facing commands
- [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md) for shipped features and sprint history
- [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) for implementation details and design constraints
- [TESTING.md](TESTING.md) for manual and automated verification guidance
- [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) when maintainers want release-note-ready entries

## Project-Specific Guidelines

### Preserve the Design Constraints

Hermes WebUI is deliberately:

- No build step
- No bundler
- No frontend framework
- Easy to modify from a terminal

Do not introduce new infrastructure or dependencies unless the gain is clear and the tradeoff is justified.

### Match the Existing Shape of the Codebase

- Server logic belongs in `api/` with `server.py` staying thin
- Frontend behavior belongs in the existing `static/*.js` modules
- Prefer extending current patterns over introducing parallel abstractions
- Keep changes legible to future contributors working directly from the repo in a terminal

### Be Careful With User-Facing Changes

This project is heavily UI-driven. If you change interaction flows, session behavior, workspace browsing, onboarding, or mobile layouts:

- test the happy path
- test reload behavior where relevant
- test narrow/mobile layouts where relevant
- include before/after images in the PR

### Security and Safety Matter

This app can expose workspace contents, run agent actions, and optionally sit behind a reverse proxy or Docker deployment. Treat auth, path handling, uploads, streaming, and environment handling as high-risk areas.

If your PR touches security-sensitive behavior, say so explicitly in the PR description and explain how you verified it.

## Writing a Good PR Message

Start with a short Thinking Path that explains the chain from project goal to the specific fix.

Example:

> - Hermes WebUI aims for near 1:1 parity with the Hermes CLI in a browser
> - Long-running chat turns rely on SSE streaming and session recovery
> - Reloading during an in-flight turn can leave the UI in an inconsistent state
> - The bug was that recovered sessions restored messages but not the live stream state
> - This PR fixes the recovery path so in-flight turns reconnect cleanly after reload
> - The benefit is that users can refresh or reconnect without losing visibility into active work

Another example:

> - Hermes WebUI is intentionally a simple Python + vanilla JS application
> - The right panel is used for workspace browsing and previews
> - On mobile, panel state changes need to be obvious and touch-friendly
> - The existing close affordance was inconsistent with the bottom-nav flow
> - This PR fixes the mobile panel close behavior and aligns it with the current navigation model
> - The result is fewer dead-end UI states on phones

After that, cover:

- what you changed
- why you changed it
- how you verified it
- what risks remain

## Review Tips

Want the smoothest review?

- Keep diffs tight
- Name things clearly
- Avoid unnecessary rewrites
- Add short comments only where the code would otherwise be hard to follow
- Respond directly to review feedback and update the PR description if the scope changes

## Development References

- [README.md](README.md)
- [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md)
- [TESTING.md](TESTING.md)
- [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md)
- [SPRINTS.md](SPRINTS.md)

Questions are best raised early, before a large change is finished.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Absorbed and shipped in **v0.51.191** (Release FK) via #3292 — your commit was cherry-picked onto the release stage with `Co-authored-by` attribution preserved. Closes #3289. Thank you @andrewkangkr! 🎉

One hardening was applied on the way in: the Codex regression gate found (by execution) that the guard blocked **any** `ctl.sh start` while the launchd job was live — including a legitimate second instance on a **different** port (e.g. `HERMES_WEBUI_PORT=8788` for a test build). Made the guard **port-aware**: `_launchd_webui_pid` now only treats the launchd job as a conflict when its PID is actually listening on the requested `CTL_PORT` (a new best-effort `_pid_listens_on_port` helper via `lsof`); a different-port start is allowed, and when `lsof` is unavailable it falls back to guarding only the default 8787 port so non-default ports are never wrongly blocked. Added a regression test that an alternate-port start is not blocked while the launchd job runs, and made your existing block test deterministic. The core fix — treating launchd as the single source of truth for the default instance — is exactly as you designed it.

payload.body:
Thanks @andrewkangkr — the pin-quota lineage fix here is real and well-targeted, but this PR currently bundles **two unrelated changes**, which is blocking it. Putting it on hold with specifics:

## Scope contamination — two logical changes in one PR

The stated fix (#3288: "pin limit counts duplicate continuation rows instead of visible lineages") is a clean, focused ~74-LOC change, and that part looks good:

- `_session_counts_toward_pin_quota()`, `_session_row_lineage_root_id()`, `_visible_pinned_lineage_ids()` in `api/routes.py`
- `tests/test_pin_limit_lineage_visibility.py` (3 tests)

But the diff **also** contains a large, unrelated **"project OS dashboard" feature** (~9 functions, ~+300 LOC): `_handle_project_os_dashboard()`, `_project_os_truth_board_slugs()`, `_project_os_resolve_repo_root_for_board()`, `.ax/handoff/current.json` / `.ax/status/*` truth-board parsing, `git_info_for_workspace` wiring, etc. None of that relates to the pin-quota bug.

This is what's driving the +401/-14 size in `routes.py` and the `CONFLICTING` state, and it trips the project's "one logical change per PR" rule (`docs/CONTRACTS.md` / `CONTRIBUTING.md`).

## To unblock

Please **split this into two PRs**:
1. **Pin-quota lineage fix only** (#3288) — just the three `_*_pin_quota` / lineage helpers + `test_pin_limit_lineage_visibility.py`, rebased on current `master`. That one is small, isolated, and we can take it quickly.
2. The **project-OS dashboard** as its own separate PR with its own description, tests, and (since it adds a new visible surface + reads `.ax/` workspace state) a UX/design pass.

If it's easier, point us at the pin-quota commit in isolation and we're happy to cherry-pick just that onto fresh master with your `Co-authored-by` attribution preserved. The lineage-dedup approach itself is sound — it's purely the bundling that's holding it up.

payload.title: fix: Windows upgrade state stranding (#2905) + gateway-configured banner (#3194)

payload.author: nesquena
payload.body:
## Review — end-to-end ✅ (clean approval, no fixes needed)

Independent review of the self-built hotfix combining #2905 (data-loss-class Windows upgrade stranding) and #3194 (two-container Docker first-deploy banner misreport). Both diagnoses match the issue threads' code citations and both fixes are surgical with exhaustive regression coverage.

### Traced against upstream hermes-agent

Pulled a fresh `nousresearch/hermes-agent` tarball at review time. Two cross-tool invariants verified:

**For #2905:** the agent itself already defaults to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` on Windows — confirmed at `hermes_cli/auth.py:4281` and `hermes_cli/auth.py:4304`. This explains why API keys survived the v0.51.134 upgrade for affected users (agent-owned `auth.json` was already at the new location) while WebUI state did not. The PR's narrow keying on **`webui/`-only markers** (not `auth.json`/`config.yaml`) is the right signal — a long-time agent-only user without WebUI legacy state can't be wrongly diverted into the legacy dir.

**For #3194:** confirmed `hermes_cli/web_server.py:633,638` writes `gateway_state = "running"` and `hermes_cli/gateway.py:834` reads it. The PR's check that `details.get("gateway_state") == "running"` or `details.get("reason") == "gateway_stale_running_state"` is precisely the agent-side signal that proves a gateway IS configured even when the freshness threshold hasn't been refreshed.

### #2905 — Windows upgrade state stranding (data-loss-class)

**End-to-end trace.**

The fix lives in two places that must agree on the base hermes home:
- [api/config.py:64-97](api/config.py#L64-L97) — `_platform_default_hermes_home()` drives `STATE_DIR` (sessions, settings, pins, UI state)
- [api/profiles.py:117-168](api/profiles.py#L117-L168) — `_resolve_base_hermes_home()` drives the active-profile pointer

After the PR, profiles.py delegates to config.py's helper (single source of truth), with a defensive ImportError fallback that preserves the original Windows logic. The two resolvers can no longer drift apart — which was a real risk because the v0.51.134 regression came from updating one without the other.

**Marker helper invariant** — verified at [api/config.py:34-61](api/config.py#L34-L61):

```python
markers = (
    base / "webui" / "sessions",
    base / "webui" / "settings.json",
    base / "webui",
)
return any(m.exists() for m in markers)
```

All three markers live inside `webui/`. An agent-only install with `auth.json` and `config.yaml` directly under `base/` cannot trigger the divert. The test `test_agent_only_artifacts_do_not_count` explicitly locks this invariant.

**Truth table** — verified by 11 tests in `test_issue2905_windows_home_migration_safety.py`, all passing:

| Scenario | Resolved to | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Upgrade fingerprint: legacy populated, new empty | **legacy** | Don't strand the user's data (the fix) ✅ |
| Fresh install: neither populated | new (`%LOCALAPPDATA%`) | Standard v0.51.134+ default ✅ |
| Already migrated: new populated | new | Don't backtrack ✅ |
| Both populated | new | Never divert an established install ✅ |
| Legacy dir exists but empty | new | No false divert ✅ |
| Explicit `HERMES_HOME` env | unchanged (override wins upstream) | Test isolation preserved ✅ |
| POSIX (non-Windows) | `~/.hermes` | Fix is Windows-only ✅ |

**Non-destructive guarantee** — `test_no_files_are_moved_by_resolution` confirms the resolver function performs zero filesystem mutations. Critical: a one-time data-move migration would itself be a data-loss vector (interrupted mid-copy, permission errors on a locked file, etc.). Pointing back at the existing data is the safe shape.

**Profiles delegation** — `test_profiles_base_home_delegates_to_config` locks the single-source-of-truth invariant. If anyone later edits config.py without profiles.py (or vice versa), this test fails loudly.

### #3194 — Gateway "not configured" banner on fresh deploy

**Root cause** (cross-repo): the PR description correctly traces this t

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
## Pre-release gate results — both reviewers clear ✅

**Full sequential suite:** `7092 passed, 7 skipped, 3 xpassed, 0 failed` (`pytest -p no:xdist`, +19 from this PR's regression tests). CI: 11/11 checks green (lint, browser-smoke, 9 test shards).

**Opus advisor:** SHIP-WITH-FIXES — confirmed both fixes correct, non-destructive, well-tested. Raised two follow-ups, both applied in this PR:
- #2905 markers narrowed to WebUI-only (`webui/`, `webui/sessions`, `webui/settings.json`) — dropped `config.yaml`/`auth.json` so a long-time agent user installing WebUI fresh isn't wrongly diverted to the legacy `%USERPROFILE%\.hermes` (agent `auth.json` predates #2897 there).
- `profiles._resolve_base_hermes_home()` `except` narrowed to `ImportError`.

**Codex regression gate:** SHIP ONLY WITH FIXES → fix applied → re-ran → **SAFE TO SHIP**. The MUST-FIX (which Opus independently flagged as Q7): treating `gateway_stale_stopped_state` as configured contradicted #1944 (a stopped root gateway should read like "not configured" so the banner doesn't nag). Now **only stale-RUNNING** metadata marks `configured=True`; stale-stopped falls through to `bool(identity_map)` like the genuinely-unconfigured case. Test updated + stale-stopped no-regression test added.

Both gates converged independently on the same finding — strong signal it was the right call.

Holding for independent review (self-built, data-loss-class). 🤖

payload.author: nesquena-hermes

payload.author: aether-agent
payload.title: fix: remove duplicate session context prefill that breaks strict chat templates (Mistral, Gemma)

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the clean, well-scoped fix. I pulled the branch and read the diff against `origin/master` plus the surrounding call chain in `api/streaming.py`. The root-cause analysis is correct and the primary change is the right one — but a few things are worth flagging before this lands so reviewers aren't working from a false sense of coverage.

## The core removal is correct

Reading `_prefill_messages_with_webui_context()` at `api/streaming.py:581` and tracing how the result is consumed at `:4703` -> `:4852`:

```python
_prefill_messages = _prefill_messages_with_webui_context(_prefill_context, _cfg)
...
prefill_messages=_prefill_messages,
```

`_prefill_messages` is handed to the agent **separately** (the `prefill_messages=` kwarg), and `_webui_session_context_message()` returns `{"role": "user", ...}`. So on a fresh turn the agent saw `system -> user(context) -> user(turn)`, which is exactly the alternation violation Mistral/Gemma reject. Removing the append fixes it.

## Concern 1 — the safety-net merge does NOT cover the prefill boundary it's described to cover

`_merge_consecutive_same_role_messages()` is only invoked inside `_sanitize_messages_for_api()` (`:2544`), and that function is applied to `conversation_history` (`:5185`, `:5410`, `:6322`) — **not** to `_prefill_messages`, which is passed raw at `:4852`. So the new helper never sees the prefill/actual-turn boundary that caused #3276. The removal at `:581` is doing 100% of the work for this bug; the merge is a backstop only for consecutive same-role pairs *already inside* `conversation_history`. Worth tightening the PR/commit wording so nobody assumes double-coverage on the prefill path.

## Concern 2 — this is not a pure duplicate; some context is dropped, not relocated

The PR rationale is "already injected via `ephemeral_system_prompt`." That's only partly true. `_webui_surface_context_prompt()` (`:211-243`) emits source/session_id/profile/workspace + recall guidance. But the removed `_webui_session_context_message()` also carried **Connected Platforms**, **Home Channels**, and the **scheduled-task delivery options** block (master `:565-578`: the `"origin"` / `"local"` / `"platform:chat_id"` delivery hints). None of that is in the ephemeral surface prompt. So for WebUI turns the agent now loses its delivery-target guidance for cron/scheduled tasks. If that guidance matters, consider folding it into `_webui_ephemeral_system_prompt()` (system role, alternation-safe) rather than dropping it outright.

## Concern 3 — latent tool_calls loss in the merge helper

At `:2470-2474`:

```python
# Keep tool_calls from the first message if the second has none,
# otherwise the second message stays as a separate entry.
if not prev.get('tool_calls') and msg.get('tool_calls'):
    prev['tool_calls'] = msg.get('tool_calls')
```

The comment says the second message "stays as a separate entry," but the code has already merged its content into `prev`. When **both** messages carry `tool_calls`, the condition is False, so the second message's `tool_calls` are silently dropped. Harmless for `user/user`, but two consecutive `assistant` messages with tool calls would lose the second call. Either append the lists, or skip merging when both sides have `tool_calls`.

## Test plan

The PR body lists unit tests (user+user, assistant+assistant, 3+ consecutive, tool preservation), but the diff is `api/streaming.py` only — no test module is included. Adding it would lock in the Concern 3 behavior; an `assistant(tool_calls) + assistant(tool_calls)` case would catch the drop above. End-to-end, the reported repro (ministral GGUF via `llama-server`, custom provider) is the right manual check.

Net: ship the `:581` removal; please reconsider whether dropping the delivery-context block is intended, and tighten the merge helper's tool_calls handling.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for this @aether-agent — the underlying bug is real and worth fixing (strict Mistral/Gemma chat templates 500 on consecutive `user` messages), and the diagnosis is good. I dug into it during a low-risk review pass and hit two blockers that need your call before it can merge. Putting it on hold with specifics:

## 1. The core fix drops real context, not just a duplicate

The PR removes the `_webui_session_context_message()` append from `_prefill_messages_with_webui_context()` on the grounds that "this context is already available in the system prompt via `_webui_ephemeral_system_prompt`." That's **partially** true but not equivalent:

- `_webui_surface_context_prompt()` (in the ephemeral prompt) covers the *session framing* (WebUI ≠ Telegram, source / session_id / profile / workspace). ✅ duplicated — safe to drop.
- `_webui_session_context_message()` **additionally enumerates connected messaging platforms and delivery targets** from `gateway_state.json` (the `platforms` loop at `api/streaming.py:527-540`). That content is **not** in the ephemeral prompt, so removing the prefill message silently drops the agent's awareness of which messaging surfaces are connected / available for delivery.

So the de-dup isn't lossless. If we want to remove the prefill message, the connected-platforms/delivery-target block should move into `_webui_surface_context_prompt()` (the ephemeral path) so that information survives.

## 2. The `_merge_consecutive_same_role_messages()` safety-net has two data-loss bugs

I reproduced both by running the helper directly:

**(a) `tool_calls` are lost when two consecutive assistant messages both carry them.** The comment says "the second message stays as a separate entry," but the code merges `cur_content` into `prev` and never appends `msg`, so the second message's `tool_calls` vanish:

```
in:  assistant(content="first",  tool_calls=[toolA])
     assistant(content="second", tool_calls=[toolB])
out: assistant(content="first\n\nsecond", tool_calls=[toolA])   # toolB LOST
```

**(b) Legitimately-distinct consecutive user turns get merged into one.** A multimodal split (`"what's in this image?"` + `[image attachment]`) or a CLI-suffix turn becomes a single user message. This is the exact data-loss class that got a recent message-merge PR (#3268) dropped from a release — a global "merge any consecutive same-role messages" on `_sanitize_messages_for_api` is too blunt a sledgehammer because it runs on *every* API call, not just the prefill edge.

## Suggested path forward

The cleanest version of this is probably:
- **Keep the core idea** of not emitting two consecutive `user` messages, but solve it at the source: if the prefill message and the actual turn are both `user`, fold the session-context into the system/ephemeral prompt (per #1 above) rather than as a `user` prefill message — then there's no consecutive-user pair to merge in the first place.
- **Drop the global `_merge_consecutive_same_role_messages()` sanitizer**, or if a defensive merge is genuinely wanted, scope it narrowly (prefill boundary only) and fix the `tool_calls` handling so no tool call is ever dropped (append `msg` as a separate entry when both sides have `tool_calls`, as the comment intends).
- Please add regression tests: (i) no two consecutive `user` messages reach the API after prefill for a WebUI turn, (ii) the connected-platforms/delivery context still reaches the model, (iii) a merge (if kept) never drops a `tool_calls` payload.

Happy to help if you'd like to pair on the ephemeral-prompt approach. No rush — closing #3276 the right way is worth getting right.

payload.title: fix: keep repaired messaging sidecar order

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
**Triage: hold + `changes-requested`** — great fix for the compression-lineage replay problem, but our pre-release regression gate (Codex GPT-5.5) caught a message-loss edge that I then reproduced empirically, so I've pulled this from the v0.51.187 batch until it's addressed. Everything else here is solid — this is one bounded fix away from mergeable.

### The bug: legitimately-repeated user messages get dropped

The new merge seeds `seen_visible` with every sidecar `(role, normalized-content)` key, then skips any CLI/state row matching one of those keys *before* prefix/suffix classification (`api/routes.py` ~L2397). When a user sends the **same visible text twice** in a session — once captured in the sidecar, again as a later CLI suffix turn — the second occurrence is silently dropped.

Minimal repro against the real function on this branch:

```python
sidecar = [user("alpha", ts=100), assistant("one", ts=101)]
cli     = [user("alpha", ts=100), assistant("one", ts=101),
           user("alpha", ts=300), assistant("two", ts=301)]   # user repeats "alpha"
out = _merged_session_messages_for_display(SimpleNamespace(messages=sidecar), cli)
# → [user "alpha", assistant "one", assistant "two"]   ← the second user "alpha" is GONE
```

### Why the stable-id escape hatch doesn't save it

The code has a guard that's *meant* to preserve a same-text row when it carries a distinct stable `id`:

```python
if not (msg_id and msg_id not in sidecar_ids and first_sidecar_ts <= timestamp <= last_sidecar_ts):
    continue
```

But `get_state_db_session_messages()` in `api/models.py` (~L3703) builds each returned row with only `role` / `content` / `timestamp` — it never copies the DB `id` column into the dict (even though the query selects it). So `msg_id` is always empty for real state.db rows, and the escape hatch is dead code in production. (The timestamp-window clause also wouldn't help the repeated-suffix case above, since that turn is *after* `last_sidecar_ts`.)

### Suggested fix

Two parts:
1. **Carry the state.db `id` into the returned message dict** in `api/models.py` `get_state_db_session_messages()` so the stable-id path is actually live.
2. **Don't suppress prefix/suffix rows on visible-key alone.** Only treat a CLI row as a duplicate of a sidecar row when their stable ids match (or when an ordered-replay / timestamp-overlap check proves the CLI row mirrors a sidecar row). A repeated user turn outside the sidecar window must survive.

Please also add a regression test: same user text once in the sidecar and again as a later CLI suffix, asserting **both** turns survive. Happy to help if the dedupe logic gets fiddly — the instinct (stop replaying old lineage rows into the tail) is exactly right, it just needs to not collapse genuine repeats. No rush.

_(For context: the rest of this batch — #3262 workspace-preview + #3250 scroll-intent — shipped in v0.51.187; this PR is held only for the above.)_

payload.author: 0zzy-tech
payload.title: fix(mcp): require authentication for write operations

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for this — I read the diff and the surrounding `mcp_server.py` to understand the full design before commenting.

## Summary

The premise is right: write operations in the MCP server currently execute without checking whether a password is even configured, so on a machine where `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD` is unset anyone can call `create_project` / `delete_project` / etc. via the MCP interface. Scoping a gate to the write tools is the correct approach.

That said, the implementation has a few issues worth addressing before this lands.

## The gate checks presence, not validity

`_require_auth()` (`mcp_server.py:551-563`) only verifies that `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD` is set:

```python
def _require_auth() -> str:
    pw = _api_password()
    if not pw:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD must be set for MCP write operations. …"
        )
    return pw
```

It does not validate the password against any stored credential, nor does it call `_api_auth()` to confirm the value is actually accepted by the server. An attacker who can set environment variables (or who simply sets `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD=anything`) bypasses the gate. The existing `_api_auth()` → `_api_post()` flow in the mutation handlers (`handle_rename_session`, `handle_move_session`) actually goes through the server's `/api/auth/login` endpoint and gets rejected with 401 if the password is wrong — so those handlers are protected at the HTTP layer. The project handlers (`handle_create_project`, `handle_rename_project`, `handle_delete_project`) write to the JSON store **directly via the filesystem** and don't go through `_api_post()`, so the HTTP layer never sees them at all. A presence check on `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD` doesn't protect those paths.

## Inconsistency with `handle_delete_project`

`handle_delete_project` (`mcp_server.py:321-386`) already has its own conditional on `_api_password()`:

```python
has_auth = bool(_api_password())
if not has_auth:
    return [TextContent(type="text", text=json.dumps({
        "ok": True,
        "deleted": proj["name"],
        "unassigned_sessions": 0,
        "warning": "Set HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD to unassign sessions; …",
    }, ensure_ascii=False))]
```

This check lets the deletion of the project record itself succeed even without auth (only the session-unassign step is blocked). The new `_require_auth()` guard added in `call_tool()` would now block `delete_project` entirely when no password is set — so the two behaviors no longer agree.

## No tests

The PR adds zero new tests. The existing `tests/test_mcp_server.py` covers `create_project` / `delete_project` / `rename_session` without touching `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD`. A reviewer has no way to confirm the gate actually fires or that the error path returns the expected JSON shape.

## Recommendation

1. For `handle_rename_session` and `handle_move_session`, a gate in `call_tool()` is probably redundant — both already call `_api_post()` which goes through `_api_auth()` → `/api/auth/login` and returns `{"error": "API 401: …"}` if auth fails. The HTTP layer already enforces it.

2. For the filesystem-write handlers (`create_project`, `rename_project`, `delete_project`): if auth enforcement is desired there, either route them through the HTTP API as well (as `rename_session` does), or document explicitly that the MCP server's security model relies on OS-level process isolation rather than password gating — the README already notes that `--profile` controls which profile's data is accessible.

3. If you keep the `call_tool()` gate, add at minimum two tests: one confirming the error JSON is returned when the env var is unset, and one confirming the handler is called normally when it is set. The existing fixture in `test_mcp_server.py:141` (`_override_env`) already provides a pattern for controlling env vars in tests.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
**Triage: hold + `changes-requested`** — the auth check as written doesn't actually authenticate the caller, and it breaks keyless setups.

Two blockers before this can land:

1. **The guard checks server-side config, not the caller's credential.** `_require_auth()` only verifies that `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD` is *set in the server's environment* — it never compares it against anything the MCP client supplied. So once a password is configured, any local process that can reach the MCP server still gets full write access to `create_project` / `delete_project` / `move_session` / etc. The threat model in the PR description ("anyone with local system access could manipulate other users' projects") is not closed by this change: the attacker with local access reads the same env or just connects to the already-authorized server. To genuinely gate writes, the tool call needs to carry a credential argument (or the transport needs to be authenticated) that is verified against the configured password — checking only that a password *exists* is security theater.

2. **It breaks every keyless MCP deployment.** Many self-hosted setups run the WebUI/MCP server without `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD` (the same keyless-is-first-class principle we shipped for LM Studio/Ollama onboarding). With this change, those users lose all write tools the moment they upgrade, with no migration path. If we do add real auth, keyless local-only setups should remain functional (e.g. gate on a bind-address / explicit opt-in, not merely password-presence).

Happy to help shape the real fix if you want to take another pass — the instinct (protect MCP writes) is right, the mechanism needs to verify the caller and preserve keyless local use. No rush.

payload.author: allenliang2022
payload.title: fix(context): scope global model.context_length to model.default only (+ live-usage-snapshot perf cache)

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
I read the full diff — `api/routes.py` (+10 lines) and `api/streaming.py` (+163 lines across four guard sites plus the `_real_ctx_cache` sentinel) — and compared it against PR #3256 (the simpler first pass on the same fix that I commented on previously).

## What this PR adds over #3256

The routes.py change is identical to #3256. The streaming.py additions have three meaningful additions beyond what #3256 proposed:

**Commit 1** re-applies the same default-only guard across all three streaming.py sites (the live-usage-snapshot loop, the session-save block, and the terminal SSE block), same as #3256.

**Commit 2** adds a `_real_ctx_cache = [None]` sentinel (`streaming.py:3920`) that resolves the real per-model context length at most once per stream inside `_live_usage_snapshot()`. This directly addresses the performance regression I flagged on #3256: without it, the guard ran a `get_config()` + `get_model_context_length()` call on every metering tick (~10×/s during streaming), freezing non-default-model streams while the default model was unaffected.

**Commit 3** adds `threshold_tokens` rescaling (`streaming.py:4028-4042`): when the real cap is applied, the threshold is multiplied by `real_cap / stale_cap` so the auto-compress trigger also reflects the real window. That's a genuine follow-up correctness fix that #3256 missed.

## Remaining concern: the `_skip_cc_cl` block still expands the pre-save region

The CI failure I described on #3256 — `test_pr1341_context_window_persistence.py` byte-budget assertion `save_call - block_start < 9000` — was caused by the `_skip_cc_cl` guard expanding the pre-save block. That guard is still present in this PR at the same location (`streaming.py:5869-5905`), and it is still ~37 lines. Unless the test was updated to widen the limit, shard 1 will still fail.

It's worth checking whether the `test_pr1341_context_window_persistence.py` assertion was bumped in this branch. The diff does not show it being touched, so if `origin/master` still has `< 9000` the break is still there.

## The `_real_ctx_cache` shape looks correct

The sentinel pattern `_real_ctx_cache = [None]` (mutable list cell so the closure can write back) with `None` / `0` / `>0` semantics is the right approach here. One minor note: the guard condition at `streaming.py:4026` is:

```python
if (
    _cl_u > 0
    and _cc_cl_u == _cl_u
    and _def_u
    and _sm_u
    and _def_u != _sm_u
):
```

This only computes the real cap when the compressor's `context_length` equals the config cap exactly. That works correctly for the described scenario (`cc.context_length == 232000 == config cap`), but would silently skip the correction if the compressor's value differed from the config cap by even 1 (e.g. after a previous partial write). It's a conservative gate — safe, just slightly narrow. Worth a comment noting the exact-match assumption.

## No tests for the new behavior

Same gap as #3256: there is no test asserting that a session on a non-default 1M model with `model.context_length: 232000` in config resolves to 1M rather than 232K in the live-usage snapshot or in the post-stream session save. The `_real_ctx_cache` caching path and the threshold-rescaling branch also have no coverage. The PR description confirms verification was done manually — locking it in a unit test (following `test_issue1436_context_indicator_load_path.py`'s MagicMock-session pattern) would prevent regression.

## Summary

The fix premise and performance cache are both correct. The threshold rescaling is a genuine improvement over #3256. The two open items are: (1) confirm whether the `test_pr1341` byte-budget assertion was widened (if not, shard 1 will still be red), and (2) add a regression test for the default-only scoping behavior and the cache path.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
**Triage: hold + `maintainer-review`** — sound idea, but this touches the streaming usage-metering hot path and needs a dedicated review pass + green CI before it can land.

Two reasons we're not folding it into a low-risk batch:

1. **CI is red on the test shard.** Shard 1 (`test (3.x, 1)`) is failing across all three Python versions. Please get that green — happy to help diagnose if it's not obvious from the run logs.

2. **The change runs inside `_live_usage_snapshot()`, which fires on every metering tick (~10×/sec during streaming).** The default-only scoping fix in `api/routes.py` (`_resolve_context_length_for_session_model`) is clean and well-motivated — a global `model.context_length` cap should not clobber a non-default model's real window. But the streaming-side perf cache (`_real_ctx_cache`) plus the threshold rescaling is non-trivial logic on a per-token path, and a regression here can freeze a stream or surface the wrong context window / auto-compress trigger. That earns a focused Opus + Codex regression pass rather than a blind merge.

The `routes.py` half is essentially ready. If you'd like, we can split the simple default-only guard from the streaming perf cache so the low-risk half lands first. For now: get shard 1 green and we'll route it for the dedicated review. (Note: superseded #3256 has been closed in favor of this PR — full credit preserved here.)

payload.author: pamnard
payload.title: Fix workspace preview closing and stale content on chat completion

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
I read the diff in full — `static/workspace.js` (+50 lines) and `static/messages.js` (+6 lines) — plus the existing `test_issue1785_workspace_preview_breadcrumb.py` to confirm the breadcrumb-navigation behavior isn't regressed.

## Summary

The fix addresses a two-part bug cleanly:

**Bug 1 (closing preview on unrelated completion):** `messages.js:1977` called `loadDir('.')` unconditionally on stream `done`, which always ended with `clearPreview({keepPanelOpen:true})` inside `loadDir()` (`workspace.js:318`). The PR changes this to `loadDir('.', { preservePreview: true })`, which skips the `clearPreview` branch. Explicit navigation (breadcrumb click, folder click) still hits `clearPreview` because those call `loadDir(path)` without `preservePreview:true` — so #1785 is preserved.

**Bug 2 (stale content after agent edits):** Preserving the preview panel when the agent *did* edit the open file would leave stale content. The PR tracks mutated paths per turn (`_turnMutatedPreviewPaths` set, populated via `noteWorkspaceMutationsFromToolCall()`) and calls `refreshOpenPreviewIfMutated()` both on `tool_complete` (`messages.js:1715`) and again after `loadDir` on `done` (`workspace.js:360`). The path matching uses `_normalizeArtifactPath()` which already exists in master, so relative-path normalization is consistent.

## Reading `refreshOpenPreviewIfMutated()`

```js
async function refreshOpenPreviewIfMutated(){
  if(typeof _previewDirty!=='undefined'&&_previewDirty) return;
  if(!_isOpenPreviewPathMutated()) return;
  if(!_previewCurrentPath||!S.session) return;
  await openFile(_previewCurrentPath, { bustCache: true });
}
```

The `_previewDirty` guard (`workspace.js:244`) is correct — it prevents a silent discard of unsaved edits. The `bustCache` option adds `&_=${Date.now()}` to the raw-file URL (`workspace.js:530`), which handles browser caching of the old content. This is correct for all four preview modes (image, audio/video, PDF, text).

## Test coverage

The new `test_workspace_preview_preserved_on_stream_done.py` has five targeted assertions:
- `preservePreview:true` is in the `done` handler's `loadDir` call
- `loadDir()` accepts and respects `preservePreview`
- `clearPreview` is still called on explicit navigation (non-`preservePreview` path)
- `resetTurnWorkspaceMutations` is called on new stream start
- `noteWorkspaceMutationsFromToolCall` is called on `tool_complete`

The existing `test_issue856_background_completion_unread.py` was updated at line 317 to search for `preservePreview` instead of `loadDir('.')` — that's the only required change and it's correct.

## One minor nit

`resetTurnWorkspaceMutations()` is called in `messages.js:687` only when `!reconnecting`. On a stream reconnect the mutation set is not cleared, so if a prior turn mutated a file and the connection dropped mid-turn, the preview would be refreshed on reconnect even if the current reconnected turn hasn't touched that file. This is probably fine in practice (a stale reload is harmless), but it's worth a comment noting the deliberate choice.

Overall this is a solid fix with appropriate tests. The logic is correct and the breadcrumb navigation contract is preserved.

payload.title: fix: suppress phantom sessions_changed after gateway restart

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for the detailed writeup. I pulled the branch and read the diff against `origin/master`, the full `_poll_loop` + `_snapshot_hash` on master, the SSE connect path in `api/routes.py`, and the gateway SSE handler in `static/sessions.js`. I think the diagnosis in the PR description doesn't match what master actually does, so I want to flag that before this goes further.

## The watcher never used mtime — notify is already hash-only
The PR says the poll loop "detect[s] state.db mtime changes and emit[s] spurious `sessions_changed` events." But on `origin/master`, `_poll_loop` (`api/gateway_watcher.py:187-192`) is already purely hash-driven:

```python
current_hash = _snapshot_hash(sessions)
if current_hash != self._last_hash:
    self._last_hash = current_hash
    self._last_sessions = sessions
    self._notify_subscribers(sessions)
```

`_snapshot_hash` keys on `session_id:updated_at:message_count` only (`gateway_watcher.py:28-34`) — mtime is never consulted. So there is no mtime-driven notification to suppress. In the new `_poll_loop`, `is_gateway_restart` only feeds a `logger.debug(...)`; the notify decision is still `if hash_changed:`. The behavior is identical to master. The 78-line `gateway_watcher.py` change is effectively a no-op for the reported symptom.

## The likely real cause is the SSE reconnect snapshot
When the gateway restarts, the browser's `EventSource('api/sessions/gateway/stream')` drops and reconnects. On every (re)connect the server unconditionally pushes an initial snapshot (`api/routes.py:7735`):

```python
initial = get_cli_sessions()
_sse(handler, 'sessions_changed', {'sessions': initial})
```

and the frontend handler re-renders the whole sidebar on any `sessions_changed` (`static/sessions.js:2800-2806`):

```js
_gatewaySSE.addEventListener('sessions_changed', (ev) => {
  ...
  if(data.sessions){
    stopGatewayPollFallback();
    renderSessionList({deferWhileInteracting:true}); // re-fetch and re-render
```

That reconnect→snapshot→`renderSessionList` cycle is what users perceive as a phantom refresh after a restart — note the existing #3103 comment right above line 7735 describing the same reconnect-thrash failure mode. If you also see a genuine new-hash notification, the more likely trigger is that `last_activity`/`message_count` actually shifts in state.db on restart, which legitimately changes `_snapshot_hash` and is not addressed here either. Either way, the mtime gate doesn't intercept these paths.

## sessions.js: dead code + duplicate write
Two issues in the `static/sessions.js` change:

1. `_restoreActiveSession` and `_clearActiveSession` (lines 111-115) are defined but never called anywhere in the PR — `grep` finds only their definitions. Dead code.
2. `_persistActiveSession(sid)` at line 608 duplicates the existing write a few lines later at master's `sessions.js:517` (`localStorage.setItem('hermes-webui-session', S.session.session_id)`), which already runs once metadata loads. The session_id is also persisted in commands.js:480, messages.js:1885/2381, and cleared/restored by boot.js:1845. The one marginal gain is persisting *before* the metadata fetch (so it survives a fetch failure), but note the 404 branch at `sessions.js:643` deliberately *clears* `hermes-webui-session` for boot-time stale IDs (#2798) — persisting eagerly at line 608 races that cleanup and could re-strand a dead session ID.

## Recommendation
I'd hold the `gateway_watcher.py` portion — it adds state and a heuristic threshold without changing the notify behavior it claims to fix. If the goal is to stop the post-restart sidebar refresh, the fix belongs on the SSE reconnect path (e.g. dedupe the initial snapshot against the client's last-known hash, or have the frontend skip `renderSessionList` when the reconnect snapshot is hash-identical to current state). Happy to look again if you can attach a repro showing the watcher emitting a notification with an unchanged `_snapshot_hash` — that would contradict my read of th

payload.author: pamnard
payload.title: fix(updates): fall through when agent release tag is not ff-reachable

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Read the diff against `origin/master`, the surrounding logic in `_check_repo_release` (`api/updates.py:513-557`) and `_select_apply_compare_ref` (`api/updates.py:469-510`), both helper predicates, and the two new tests. The fix is correct and lands at the right layer — this is a WebUI-side updater concern, not an agent contract issue.

## The gap you're closing is real
The two existing fall-through clauses cover (a) `behind == 0 && HEAD past tag` (#2653/#2846) and (b) `behind > 0 && HEAD contains tag` (#3140). Neither covers diverged histories where the latest tag is neither an ancestor nor a descendant of HEAD. In that state the banner advertises `v2026.5.29 -> v2026.5.29.2` but the apply path runs `git pull --ff-only v2026.5.29.2`, which fails. Adding the ff-reachability gate aligns check and apply with what git can actually do.

## One observation: the new clause subsumes the #3140 clause
In `_check_repo_release`, given `behind > 0` (so `current_tag != latest_tag`, i.e. `HEAD != latest_tag`):

```python
if behind > 0 and _head_contains_ref(path, latest_tag):      # #3140
    return None
if behind > 0 and not _can_fast_forward_to(path, latest_tag): # this PR
    return None
```

`_head_contains_ref(tag)` is `merge-base --is-ancestor tag HEAD` (tag is an ancestor of HEAD). `_can_fast_forward_to(tag)` is `merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD tag` (HEAD is an ancestor of tag). If the tag is an ancestor of HEAD and `HEAD != tag`, then HEAD cannot be an ancestor of the tag, so `not _can_fast_forward_to` is always True. The new clause therefore catches every case the #3140 clause does, plus the diverged case. That's not a bug — keeping both is harmless and the #3140 clause is more self-documenting — but worth noting that the new gate is the more general predicate. If you ever consolidate, you could drop the #3140 line and keep the ff check alone.

## Case-D regression check passes
I traced `test_select_apply_compare_ref_case_d_older_tag_with_commits_and_newer_tag_exists` (`tests/test_updates.py:610`) against your new clause. Its `fake_git` has a catch-all `return '', True`, so the new `merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD v2026.5.16` resolves to ok=True → `_can_fast_forward_to` True → `not ...` False → the clause does **not** fire, and the apply still correctly targets `v2026.5.16`. So a genuinely ff-reachable newer tag is still advertised and applied as a tag. Good — the tradeoff in your "Risks" note (release-line checkout with local commits + unreachable newer tag now falls through to branch) is the correct behavior since `--ff-only` to that tag would fail anyway.

## Test coverage
The two new tests pin both the check side and apply side of the diverged-history scenario with realistic `describe`/`merge-base` stubs, and you updated `_fake_git_for_release_fetch_failure` to answer the new `merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD <tag>` probe so the existing fetch-failure test keeps passing. That's the right shape. (Per cron policy I don't execute PR code, so this is a static read — but the stub coverage looks complete: every `_run_git` arg combo the two functions can hit is answered.)

LGTM on the logic. The only thing I'd consider is the subsumption note above; otherwise this is ready.

payload.author: allenliang2022
payload.title: fix(context): scope global model.context_length to model.default only

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for this — I read the diff against `origin/master`, the resolver in `api/routes.py`, the four guard blocks in `api/streaming.py`, and the agent-side contract. The core premise is correct, but I can pin down exactly why CI shard 1 is red on every Python version.

## The fix premise is right
`agent/model_metadata.py:1485-1486` (agent side) treats `config_context_length` as an unconditional step-0 override:

```python
# 0. Explicit config override — user knows best
if config_context_length is not None and isinstance(config_context_length, int) and config_context_length > 0:
    return config_context_length
```

So forwarding the global `model.context_length` for *every* model genuinely clobbers per-model metadata. Scoping it to `model.default` in `_resolve_context_length_for_session_model` (`api/routes.py:2048-2057`) is the correct layer, and that helper still carries the `config_context_length=`, `provider=`, `custom_providers=`, and `except TypeError:` kwargs that `test_issue1896_context_length_fallback_args.py` pins — so the routes.py change is safe.

## Why shard 1 fails (deterministic, not flaky)
The break is in `api/streaming.py`, not `routes.py`. `test_pr1341_context_window_persistence.py:46` asserts the post-merge save block stays under a byte budget:

```python
save_call = src.find("\n                s.save()", block_start)
...
assert save_call - block_start < 9000, (
    "s.save() should be close to the post-merge marker — block expanded unexpectedly. "
    "If you've added a new pre-save mutation block here, bump this limit.")
```

Measured on the two trees, the span from the `if _reasoning_text and s.messages:` marker to `s.save()`:
- `origin/master`: **8688 bytes** (just under 9000)
- this PR's HEAD: **11431 bytes**

The ~37-line `_skip_cc_cl` guard you inserted before `s.save()` pushes it over the limit. `pytest-shard` partitions by test-id hash, so this test lands in shard 1 on 3.11/3.12/3.13 alike — matching `test (3.11, 1)`, `(3.12, 1)`, `(3.13, 1)` all FAILURE while shards 0/2 stay green.

## Recommendation
Two options, in order of preference:

1. **Extract a helper.** You've added four near-identical guard blocks (streaming.py:3990-4030, ~5837-5862, ~6076-6101, plus the two fallback `_apply_cfg_ctx` gates). Collapsing them into one `_compressor_context_length(agent, cfg, resolved_model, resolved_provider)` keeps the pre-save block small (stays under 9000), removes the duplication, and is easier to test directly. The inline block at streaming.py:3990 also omits `custom_providers=` in its recompute call while the SSE/save paths rely on the existing fallback resolver that does pass it — a helper would make that consistent.

2. If you keep it inline, bump the `< 9000` limit in `test_pr1341_context_window_persistence.py:46` (the assertion message explicitly invites this) and add a regression test for the new behavior — a session on a non-default 1M model with global `context_length: 232000` set should resolve to 1M, not 232K. There's no test in the PR covering the actual fix yet.

A focused unit test asserting the default-only scoping (mirroring `test_issue1436_context_indicator_load_path.py`'s MagicMock-session style) would also lock the behavior in.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
I read the diff and checked the current `api/updates.py:159-184` on `origin/master` to confirm the tests match the actual implementation.

## What the tests cover

Both new tests in `tests/test_updates.py` correctly target the implementation on master:

**`test_run_git_uses_utf8_replacement_for_windows_console_output`** — asserts that `subprocess.run` is called with `encoding='utf-8'` and `errors='replace'`. The actual call at `updates.py:165-170` is:

```python
r = subprocess.run(
    ['git'] + args, cwd=str(cwd), capture_output=True,
    text=True, timeout=timeout,
    encoding='utf-8', errors='replace',
)
```

The assertion `kwargs['encoding'] == 'utf-8'` and `kwargs['errors'] == 'replace'` pins this exactly. If a future refactor drops either kwarg (the pre-fix behavior that caused crashes on GBK locales), the test fails.

**`test_run_git_handles_missing_stdout_after_decode_thread_failure`** — passes `stdout=None` and asserts the return is `('', True)`. The actual guard at `updates.py:175`:

```python
stdout = (r.stdout or '').strip()
```

This produces `''` for `None`, so `return stdout, True` → `('', True)`. The test correctly pins this defensive path.

## Fit with existing test patterns

The two new tests follow the same `patch('subprocess.run')` + `MagicMock(returncode=…, stdout=…, stderr=…)` pattern used by the existing `test_run_git_returns_stderr_on_failure`, `test_run_git_returns_stdout_when_no_stderr`, and `test_run_git_returns_exit_code_when_no_output` at lines 132-170. `test_run_git_uses_utf8_replacement_for_windows_console_output` accesses `mock_run.call_args.kwargs`. This works in Python ≥ 3.8 (when `call_args.kwargs` was added as a named-attribute accessor). payload.author: camr
payload.title: fix: resolve 564 ruff lint errors across Python source files

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Thanks for this, @camr — running the whole tree through ruff was a real effort and the intent (cleaner, more maintainable code) is one we share. We're going to **close this PR**, but with a concrete forward plan rather than a flat no — here's the full reasoning so it's transparent.

## Why not merge this as-is

1. **The repo doesn't currently run ruff** (no `[tool.ruff]` config, no ruff in CI), so these 564 fixes are compliance for a linter we don't yet enforce — the *ongoing* value only exists once there's a gate keeping new code clean.
2. **`--unsafe-fixes` across 194 files is high-blast-radius for cosmetic gain.** I ran ruff 0.15.10 on current master to ground this: of the 600 findings, the correctness-class rules find essentially nothing real — E9 (syntax/runtime) is **clean**, and the 2 F821 undefined-name hits are both false positives (a `"CredentialPool"` forward-reference annotation and a synchronously-evaluated `lambda` over an `except ... as e`). The 600 are F401 unused-import (303), F841 unused-var (65), E402/E701/E741 style, etc. — all tidy-tier. So this is not catching latent bugs; it's reformatting.
3. **The branch is ~1805 commits behind master**, so absorbing it means a 194-file conflict resolution that would also collide with every other open PR.

## The forward plan (filed as a tracked issue)

The durable value isn't a one-time reformat — it's a **gate that keeps *new* code clean going forward**. I've opened an issue to adopt ruff properly:
- a curated `[tool.ruff]` config (correctness-focused: pyflakes + bugbear, not blanket style churn),
- ruff in CI (`tests.yml`) **and** as a pre-release pre-gate,
- scoped so it's green on master day one and only flags newly-introduced violations — no big-bang reformat required.

Whether to *also* retroactively clean all existing code (the work this PR did) is a separate, deliberate decision the maintainer wants to take on its own terms — and if we go there, it'll be a maintainer-run **safe-fixes-only** pass on fresh master, not an `--unsafe-fixes` bulk merge.

Your work here directly informed that plan — thank you for surfacing it. Closing in favor of the tracked adoption issue.

payload.author: allenliang2022
payload.title: fix(updates): prevent startup crash on non-UTF-8 (GBK) locales

payload.author: allenliang2022
payload.body:
@nesquena when you get a chance, would you mind taking a look? This is a small, self-contained startup-crash fix for non-UTF-8 (GBK) Windows locales — `_run_git` decoded git output with the locale codepage, so the binary `git diff --binary HEAD` in `_dirty_suffix` raised `UnicodeDecodeError`, leaving `r.stdout = None` and crashing `import api.updates` before the server could bind its port. One-file change (+6 / −2), forcing UTF-8 with `errors='replace'`.

I don't have permission to set labels on this repo, but `bug` seems like the right fit if you agree. Thanks!

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Pulled this into a read-only worktree and read `api/updates.py` at HEAD against `origin/master`. The diagnosis holds up end-to-end, and the fix is in the right place.

## What I verified

`_run_git()` on master (`api/updates.py:159-180`) calls `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` with no explicit `encoding`, so Python decodes the child's stdout using the locale-preferred codec — GBK on Chinese Windows. The crash path you describe is real and reachable at import time:

```python
out = _describe_git_version(REPO_ROOT)   # api/updates.py:229
...
WEBUI_VERSION: str = _detect_webui_version()   # api/updates.py:355 — MODULE LEVEL
```

Because `WEBUI_VERSION` is computed at module scope, any exception out of `_run_git` propagates through `import api.updates` and takes the process down before the port is bound — exactly the "something is killing the server" symptom that's hard to attribute.

The trigger is `_dirty_suffix()` at `api/updates.py:198`, which runs the **binary** diff:

```python
diff, diff_ok = _run_git(['diff', '--binary', 'HEAD', '--'], path, timeout=timeout)
```

Binary diff output legitimately contains bytes that aren't valid GBK, so `text=True` raises `UnicodeDecodeError` in the reader thread and leaves `r.stdout = None`, after which `r.stdout.strip()` raises `AttributeError`. Confirmed.

## On the fix

Forcing `encoding='utf-8', errors='replace'` plus the `(r.stdout or '')` guard is the correct, minimal fix, and it's self-consistent with code that already exists one function down — `_dirty_suffix` hashes the diff with `hashlib.sha1(diff.encode('utf-8', errors='replace'))` at `api/updates.py:200`, so byte-exactness of the binary diff was never relied on here. The `errors='replace'` therefore can't regress the `-dirty-<digest>` suffix beyond what the encode step already tolerated.

One thing worth confirming since `_run_git` is the shared primitive for *all* git calls in this module (≈30 call sites — `describe`, `fetch`, `pull`, `stash`, `reset --hard` in the update flow): none of them depend on byte-exact stdout, they all `.strip()` text and compare/parse it, so `errors='replace'` is safe across the board, not just for the version probe. The `(r.stderr or '')` guard is a good belt-and-suspenders addition for the same `None`-stream case.

## Verification suggestion

A cheap regression guard would assert `_run_git` passes `encoding='utf-8'`/`errors='replace'` (a source-level assertion, in the spirit of the existing `tests/` string checks), so a future refactor that drops the encoding can't silently reintroduce the locale-dependent crash. Not a blocker — the change is correct as-is.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Read both touched files at HEAD against `origin/master` and traced the autofill → phantom-toast path. The fix is correct and lands in both DOM sources, which matters here.

## Why the phantom toast happens

`_stashClarifyDraft()` (`static/messages.js:2973`) reads the input value unconditionally and, if non-empty, both appends it to the composer and fires the toast:

```js
const draft = String((input && input.value) || "").trim();
if (!draft) return false;
...
: "Clarification closed. Your draft was kept in the composer.";   // messages.js:2996
```

`hideClarifyCard()` calls `_stashClarifyDraft(reason)` on teardown (`static/messages.js:3032`). So if Chrome's password manager has silently autofilled `#clarifyInput` with a saved base-URL credential, `draft` is non-empty even though the user never opened a clarify card — the session-complete teardown then stashes that URL into the composer and shows "Clarification closed." Diagnosis confirmed.

## On the fix

`autocomplete="off"` alone is known-insufficient against Chrome's heuristic credential matcher; the `readonly` + `onfocus="this.removeAttribute('readonly')"` pattern is the standard reliable workaround, since Chrome skips readonly fields. Patching **both** `static/index.html:498` and the `_ensureClarifyCardDom()` template (`static/messages.js:2837`) is the right call — the dynamic builder shadows the static markup whenever the card is recreated, so a one-sided patch would regress on whichever path actually constructs the live DOM.

The programmatic `input.removeAttribute('readonly')` inside `showClarifyCard()` (`static/messages.js:3140`) closes the loop for the keyboard-only / focus-via-choice case: when a real prompt arrives, the field is made writable even if the user reaches it through the "Other" button's `el.focus()` (`messages.js` choices block) rather than a pointer click, so the `onfocus` handler isn't the only thing that can clear `readonly`.

## One small note

There's overlap with #3245, which also touches `showClarifyCard()` (adding `clarify_id` to the dedupe signature). The two changes are orthogonal — different lines, no conflict in intent — but whichever merges second will want a trivial rebase. Worth a maintainer noting so they land cleanly.

CI is green across all 3.11/3.12/3.13 shards plus browser-smoke, which is the relevant gate for a static-asset change. No further verification needed from my side.

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Read `showClarifyCard()` at HEAD against `origin/master` and cross-checked the linked issue #3241. The one-line signature change is targeted and correct.

## Why the stale card persists

On master the dedupe signature deliberately excludes `clarify_id`:

```js
const sig = JSON.stringify({
  question,
  choices,
  sid: pending._session_id || (S.session && S.session.session_id) || null,
});   // static/messages.js:2985-2989
```

That `sig` then drives the `sameClarify` short-circuit:

```js
const sameClarify = card.classList.contains("visible") && _clarifySignature === sig;
...
if (!sameClarify) input.value = '';   // messages.js:3138
```

So when a second clarify prompt is *text-identical* to one whose response was already accepted (same question, same choices, same session), `sameClarify` is `true`. The card is treated as the same prompt: `_clarifyVisibleSince` isn't reset, the input value isn't cleared, and the previously submitted text stays visible — exactly the #3241 repro ("popup can stay open and keep the submitted input visible").

## On the fix

Adding `clarify_id: pending.clarify_id || null` to the signature is the right discriminator. `_clarifyId` is already tracked separately (set right below at `showClarifyCard`, reset in `_resetClarifyCardState()`), so folding it into `sig` makes the dedupe key match the identity the rest of the card state already uses. A genuinely-new prompt now produces a distinct `sig`, flips `sameClarify` to `false`, and the `if (!sameClarify)` branches correctly clear the input and reset the visibility timer.

The `|| null` fallback is important: prompts that arrive without a `clarify_id` collapse to the prior behavior (question/choices/sid only), so this can't regress the legitimate "same prompt re-rendered" coalescing case.

## On the test

`tests/test_sprint30.py` asserting the literal `'clarify_id: pending.clarify_id || null'` is in the `showClarifyCard` body is consistent with the existing source-assertion style in that file (it already checks for `JSON.stringify` and `_clarifySignature`). It's brittle to reformatting but cheap, and it does guard the specific regression.

## Coordination note

#3247 also edits `showClarifyCard()` (adds `input.removeAttribute('readonly')` for the autofill fix). Different lines, no semantic conflict — but whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase. CI is green here across all shards + browser-smoke.

payload.title: test: skip terminal cleanup collection on non-POSIX hosts

payload.author: nesquena-hermes
payload.body:
Reading `tests/test_terminal_process_cleanup.py` on `origin/master` against this diff, the fix is correct and minimal.

## Why the guard is needed
`api/terminal.py` imports `fcntl` (and `termios`) unconditionally at module load:

```python
# api/terminal.py:11-22
import errno
import atexit
import codecs
import fcntl          # ← POSIX-only, raises ModuleNotFoundError on Windows
...
import termios        # ← also POSIX-only
```

Since the test does `import api.terminal as terminal` at module top, pytest **collection** triggers that import chain and dies on a non-POSIX host before any test body runs. The existing per-test guard at `tests/test_terminal_process_cleanup.py:74-75`:

```python
@pytest.mark.skipif(
    not hasattr(os, "openpty") or os.name != "posix",
```

is a `skipif` *marker* — it only takes effect once the test function is selected, which is too late: collection already failed at the module import. So the module-level `pytest.skip(..., allow_module_level=True)` placed **before** `import api.terminal` is exactly the right level to short-circuit collection. The new guard and the existing marker are redundant on POSIX (both pass through) and complementary on non-POSIX (module skip wins first).

## Verdict
- Test-only change, no runtime/behavior impact on POSIX hosts — the import and all lifecycle assertions are unchanged there.
- `allow_module_level=True` is required for a top-level `pytest.skip` and is present.
- Placement before the `api.terminal` import is correct; moving it after would not help.

LGTM. The only nit: the diff adds the guard but the redundant `os.name != "posix"` clause in the line-74 `skipif` could later be simplified to just `not hasattr(os, "openpty")`, since the module skip now handles the non-POSIX case — but that's cosmetic and not worth blocking on.
